home.name: Our hostel
home.note: Where we are staying. Not a sight.

sights.name: Catholic church of the Transfiguration
sights.blurb: Look at the east wall of this brick church on Str. Mihai Eminescu: three projectile tubes are set into the masonry.
sights.q: Catholic church of the Transfiguration, Vatra Dornei

sights.name: Primăria and heroes' monument
sights.blurb: The town hall (1897, in a Florentine palazzo style) and the obelisk in the park beside it are the civic centre of the Habsburg town.
sights.q: Primăria and heroes' monument, Vatra Dornei

sights.name: Heroes' cemetery
sights.blurb: A terraced war cemetery on the hillside near Gara Mare: rows of plain concrete crosses, nearly all reading Erou Necunoscut (Unknown Hero), under a tall oak cross of 1937.

sights.name: Catholic cemetery: the Austrian soldier's grave
sights.blurb: Among the graves is a crude stone cross that locals call "the Austrian soldier's grave".
sights.q: Catholic cemetery: the Austrian soldier's grave, Vatra Dornei

sights.name: Gara Mare (Vatra Dornei station)
sights.blurb: The main station of 1902, where the railway first reached Dorna, is also the town's place of departure in the worst sense.

sights.name: Great Synagogue
sights.blurb: A large, decaying synagogue of about 1898–1902 on Str. Mihai Eminescu, visible from three sides and not in use.

sights.name: Jewish cemetery
sights.blurb: On the slope along Str. Negrești, the cemetery of the community that helped build the spa.

sights.name: Bradul–Călimani spa hotels
sights.blurb: These two big hotels at the foot of the ski slope, Bradul (312 beds) and Călimani (about 290), are joined by a corridor to a 2,190 m² treatment base.

sights.name: Casa Vladimir
sights.blurb: This listed building at the start of Str. Mihai Eminescu sums up the town's owners in one façade.

sights.name: Former Hotel Dorna
sights.blurb: The listed hotel at the corner of Eminescu and Gării is a building out of use.

sights.name: Mestecăniș tunnel
sights.blurb: The railway into Vatra Dornei passes under the Mestecăniș ridge through a crest tunnel of about 1,622 m (1,646.6 m with portals), opened in October 1902 by the Bukovina local railway company.
sights.when: In use; see from the train.

sights.name: Călimani sulphur quarry and the ghost colony
sights.blurb: High above Gura Haitii, at about 1,500–2,000 m, the communist state cut away the side of a volcano.
sights.when: Abandoned; 12–15 km rough concrete road; snow from Nov.
sights.q: Călimani sulphur quarry and the ghost colony

sights.name: Arșița manganese quarry, Iacobeni
sights.blurb: On the hillside above Iacobeni is a quarry about 2.4 km² across, opened into old manganese workings, with at least three gallery mouths showing in its walls.
sights.when: Parts may be active; outside only.

sights.name: Manz manor, Iacobeni
sights.blurb: In Iacobeni stands the abandoned manor, built in 1823, of the family that founded modern mining in Bukovina, with its service pavilion in the same state.

sights.name: Cârlibaba: the Polish Legion grave
sights.blurb: Beside the hillside Catholic church of Cârlibaba Nouă is a mass grave of Polish Legion soldiers: Captain Stanisław Strzelecki and eleven legionaries, killed in January 1915 fighting the Russians for the Carpathian passes.

sights.name: Dorna bottling plant, Poiana Negrii
sights.blurb: The factory that fills Romania's best-known mineral water.

sights.name: Casino (Cazinoul Băilor)
sights.blurb: The pale palace between the park and the river is the building the whole town was arranged around.

sights.name: Sentinela spring
sights.blurb: The little tower behind the Casino is the town's emblem: a spring pavilion of 1896 over a spring found in 1871.

sights.name: Unirea spring and the old bath house
sights.blurb: These two 1890s buildings on Str. Republicii are where the cure actually happened.
sights.q: Unirea spring and the old bath house, Vatra Dornei

sights.name: Parcul Balnear
sights.blurb: The spa park behind the Casino is a 50 ha dendrological reserve and the town's main cluster of springs.

sights.name: Gara Vatra Dornei Băi
sights.blurb: The small station in the centre, "Băi" meaning "Baths", was built in 1910 on the left bank of the Dorna so that spa guests could step off the train almost at the Casino door.
sights.q: Gara Vatra Dornei Băi, Vatra Dornei

sights.name: Natural Sciences and Hunting Museum
sights.blurb: A small museum of the Dorna basin's animals and plants, founded in 1956 and reopened in September 2026 after an energy refit.

sights.name: Holy Trinity Cathedral
sights.blurb: The large Orthodox cathedral at the entrance to the spa park, built 1991–2002, with seven towers for the seven sacraments.

sights.name: St Elias wooden church
sights.blurb: A small wooden church in a cemetery yard on the way up to the chairlift.
sights.q: St Elias wooden church, Vatra Dornei

sights.name: Nativity of the Virgin church
sights.blurb: An Orthodox church in Moldavian style that started life as the Lutheran church of Dorna's Germans, built in 1905.
sights.q: Nativity of the Virgin church, Vatra Dornei

sights.name: Dealul Negru chairlift
sights.blurb: A 1980 chairlift that climbs about 3 km from 860 m to about 1,300 m in roughly 25 minutes of open chairs.

sights.name: Șaru Dornei: the arsenic springs
sights.blurb: South of Gura Negrei, between Șarul peak and the Sărișorul brook, is a walled hollow where carbon dioxide rises through the water in large bubbles: the La Cruce ("At the Cross") spring.
sights.when: Springs used locally; plant reportedly gone.

sights.name: Călimani National Park visitor centre
sights.blurb: A small centre in Șaru Dornei on the Călimani volcano: a big model of the 10 km caldera, panels on the rock layers and vegetation belts, and a section on why the basin's mineral waters form here, with tastings of local waters.

sights.name: Dorna Candrenilor: the spa that came back
sights.blurb: A village spa about 7 km west that died in the 1930s and reopened in the 2020s.
sights.q: Dorna Candrenilor: the spa that came back

sights.name: Ciocănești: the painted village and egg museum
sights.blurb: A village on the Golden Bistrița where more than 600 houses are painted outside with the patterns of local costume and painted eggs.
sights.q: Ciocănești: the painted village and egg museum

sights.name: Tihuța Pass: Castel Dracula and the war railway
sights.blurb: At 1,201 m on the road to Bistrița stands a mock-medieval hotel, built in 1976–83 as Hotel Tihuța to cash in on Bram Stoker's "Borgo Pass".
sights.q: Tihuța Pass: Castel Dracula and the war railway

sights.name: Tinovul Mare peat bog
sights.blurb: A 681 ha raised peat bog at Poiana Stampei, 8,000–9,000 years old, crossed by a wooden boardwalk of about 900 m.

sights.name: Vila Belvedere ("Casa Blaga")
sights.blurb: This villa on the street now named after the poet-philosopher Lucian Blaga is the town's main literary claim.

sights.name: Casa de Cultură "Platon Pardău"
sights.blurb: The town's cultural centre since 1952, opposite the Primăria, named after Platon Pardău (1934–2002), a poet and prose writer born in Vatra Dornei.
sights.q: Casa de Cultură "Platon Pardău", Vatra Dornei

sights.name: Pavilionul Japonez, the busts and the squirrels
sights.blurb: The 1925 bandstand by the lake in the spa park, the alley of writers' busts and the park's famous tame squirrels.
sights.q: Pavilionul Japonez, Parcul Central, Vatra Dornei

sights.name: Dealul Runc viewpoint
sights.blurb: The closest real viewpoint over the town: a 20–25 minute climb up Runc hill, the first summit of the Suhard ridge.
sights.when: Free. Muddy or icy after rain or snow.

sights.name: Veverița and Parc ski slopes
sights.blurb: The town's two in-town ski runs: Veverița (850 m, lit at night) and the beginners' Parc slope right by the centre.
sights.when: Winter only: closed in November; opens late Dec–Jan with snow.

sights.name: Casa Bucovineană (restaurant)
sights.blurb: The restaurant locals and guides name first for Bukovinian food, with live traditional music.

sights.name: St Demetrius Monastery
sights.blurb: A modern convent at the town's eastern exit, on the site of an old hermitage.

sights.name: Dorna Arini wooden monastery
sights.blurb: An all-timber convent 5 km east of town, with a tall wooden bell tower: locals call it a pity to miss.
sights.q: Mănăstirea Acoperământul Maicii Domnului Dorna Arini

sights.name: Cheile Zugrenilor (Zugreni gorges)
sights.blurb: The most spectacular stretch of the Bistrița: walls 200–300 m high, about 20 km downstream on DN17B.
sights.when: Seen from the road, open all year; rafting off-season.

sights.name: Rarău: Pietrele Doamnei and Rarău monastery
sights.blurb: The limestone towers of "the Lady's Rocks", up to 70 m tall above 1,600 m on the Rarău plateau, with a monastery founded by Petru Rareș nearby.
sights.when: Use the Pojorâta road (kept open); the Chiril road closes in winter.

sights.name: Câmpulung Moldovenesc: Wood Art and spoon museums
sights.blurb: Bukovina's wood culture in two museums: 15,000 wooden objects at the Arta Lemnului, and a teacher's collection of 6,000 spoons.
sights.when: Arta Lemnului Tue–Sun 9–17 (winter), 20 lei. Spoons: donation, phone ahead.

sights.name: Voroneț: the "Sistine Chapel of the East"
sights.blurb: The most famous of Bukovina's UNESCO painted churches, known for its Last Judgement and its "Voroneț blue".

sights.name: Humor monastery
sights.blurb: A UNESCO painted church known for its red-ochre tones, a short drive from Voroneț.

sights.name: Moldovița monastery
sights.blurb: Petru Rareș's 1532 painted church, the nearest of the UNESCO monasteries to Vatra Dornei, famous for its Siege of Constantinople.

sights.name: Sucevița monastery
sights.blurb: The last and largest of the painted churches, a fortified monastery famous for its Ladder of Virtues.

sights.name: Putna monastery
sights.blurb: The burial place of Stephen the Great, Moldavia's national hero; not a painted church, but the country's great pilgrimage site.

sights.name: 12 Apostoli rocks, Călimani
sights.blurb: Volcanic rock pillars at about 1,760 m that look like faces and figures, reached by a themed trail from Gura Haitii.
sights.when: Clear, snow-free days only; 4–6 h hike; start by 9:00.

sights.name: Vârful Oușoru (Suhard)
sights.blurb: The distinctive 1,639 m peak that dominates the basin: locals read the weather from its crest.
sights.when: Hike from town; upper part may be snowy in November.

offmap.name: Oița manganese mine, Ciocănești
offmap.blurb: The only manganese mine in Romania you can enter: a gallery near Ciocănești where you put on rubber boots, a helmet and a miner's lamp and walk into rock at 3 °C.
offmap.when: Groups only, by appointment through the Țara Dornelor tourism office. Near Ciocănești, about 20 km north-west.

p: The pale palace between the park and the river is the building the whole town was arranged around. It was built in 1896–98 by the Viennese architect Peter Paul Brang and opened on 10 July 1899, at the height of Dorna-Watra's career as a Habsburg spa. Inside are a restored ballroom with gilded stucco and chandeliers, photo rooms on the Austro-Hungarian resort, and a brick-vaulted basement gallery.

The casino came out of a lobbying campaign by Mayor Vasile Deac (mayor 1875–1902), who won the case for it at an audience with Emperor Franz Joseph. It was modelled on a fashionable Baden casino; sources disagree on whether that means Baden bei Wien or Baden-Baden. In 1895 Dorna had become the first electrified town in Bukovina, and the casino, the bath house, the spring pavilions and Hotel Carol were all built in the same few years. Until the late 1930s, guests came from Vienna, Berlin and Budapest.

Its second life is just as telling. It was nationalised on 11 June 1948 and turned into a workers' club, with party meetings, union events and even national chess championships. A 1960s extension turned part of it into a canteen. It was closed in 1988 as unsafe, then sat for thirty years as a ruin. It was returned to the Orthodox Church Fund of Bukovina in 2004, restored with EU money from 2019 to 2023, and reopened on 28 November 2023.

Practical: Wednesday to Sunday. The official site says 11:00–18:00, but Google lists 12:00–16:00, so call 0744 422 733. Entry is said to cost about 20 lei (unconfirmed). Labels are in Romanian only. The famous list of visitors (Iorga, Crainic and others) has no traceable source, so treat it as tradition.
casino.s: cazinoul-bailor.ro; Europa Liberă (2022); Adevărul; Ziua Bucovinei (Nov 2023)

p: The little tower behind the Casino is the town's emblem: a spring pavilion of 1896 over a spring found in 1871. Its names tell the century's politics. It was first "Falkenhayn", after a Habsburg agriculture minister. From 1944 to 1989 it was "23 August", the date of Romania's switch to the Allies, which the communists made the national day. After 1989 it became "Sentinela", the sentry.

The chemistry is the real story. Dorna's waters are ordinary groundwater from the river terraces, calcium–magnesium bicarbonate water like the local fresh water. What makes them "mineral" is carbon dioxide rising from depth and dissolving into them: the gas makes the water acidic enough to pick up iron and other minerals. The region counts dozens of such carbonated springs. In 1857 Dorna's iron springs were measured as richer in iron than those of the Styrian spa Gleichenberg. The first scientific notes on the area's waters come from Balthasar Hacquet's travels in 1788–89. Sources disagree on whether the 1805 analysis of the town's springs was Hacquet's or Pluschk's.

Today the tower is often shut and has housed a shop. Visitors fill bottles from a source just behind it, and the water is drinkable. The site has been criticised as neglected; ro.wikipedia even records journalists finding people relieving themselves beside the monument. Two other spa-era springs, Ferdinand (1899) and the "Izvorul de Sus" pavilion, are mentioned in the sources, but their state today is unknown.
sentinela.s: ro.wikipedia "Izvorul Sentinela"; dragusanul.ro; redescopera-taradornelor.ro; geochemical study (copy on pdfcoffee); Google reviews (2025–26)

unirea-spring.t: Unirea spring and the old bath house
p: These two 1890s buildings on Str. Republicii are where the cure actually happened. The Unirea spring house (1896, a listed monument) stands over what was once the "Ioan" well. In the early 1800s patients carried water from it to their lodgings and bathed at home. Next door, the bath house held cabins for iron-water baths and peat-mud packs. Today the spring building is the Maestro restaurant and hostel.

The spa grew in stages. After 1830 a Viennese doctor found that the local peat mud helped rheumatism. In 1870 the Church Fund of Bukovina bought the baths and the water rights. In 1883 Franz Joseph approved its plan for a resort of European standard. The 1890s building boom followed: bath house, spring houses, Casino, Hotel Carol, Primăria, then the railway. "Ioan" became "Unirea" (Union) in a later renaming.

Look at the pair as a set with Hotel Carol (1896, originally the spa's first treatment villa, a hotel since 2002) and the Casino. Together they are the surviving core of the Habsburg spa. The bath doctor Arthur Loebel (born 1857) wrote its first history in 1896. Don't come for the restaurant: reviews are poor.
unirea-spring.s: LMI (SV-II-m-B-05669 and others); dornaecoturism.ro; romania-travel-guide.com; Europa Liberă file on the Casino restoration (2022)

p: These two big hotels at the foot of the ski slope, Bradul (312 beds) and Călimani (about 290), are joined by a corridor to a 2,190 m² treatment base. They are the other face of the spa: the mass, state-referral cure, where patients come with a doctor's note and a health card for carbonated baths, mud and paraffin wraps, and the mofette, a dry bath in natural carbon dioxide gas.

The contrast with the Casino is the point. The Habsburg spa was built for a few hundred wealthy guests. The socialist spa was built to process trade-union members in shifts. Treatment still runs on weekdays only. The construction date and architect could not be confirmed. The "communist-era" label rests on the scale and the model, not on a document.

Guest reviews describe fixed meal times, heating you cannot control and policies "unchanged since 1977". That is anecdote, but it fits. The pool may sell day passes (one listing says Tue–Sun 12:00–23:00); ask at reception.

This villa on the street now named after the poet-philosopher Lucian Blaga is the town's main literary claim. It opened in spring 1931 and was registered as "Casa Blaga" in 1936. Today it is a hotel and restaurant, so you can actually sit here: open 7:30–22:00.

The hotel's own story says that Blaga lived here from 1952 to 1964, finishing his Goethe Faust translation and his Lessing volumes. That cannot be right as written. Blaga died in Cluj on 6 May 1961. After the communists removed him from his chair in 1948 he worked in Cluj as a librarian, publishing only translations. The villa itself was nationalised on 11 June 1948 and run by the state spa enterprise. So the 1950s residence is hotel lore. Stays in the 1930s, when the house bore his name, are plausible, and local writers link the Dorna valley to his early poems. Who exactly built and owned the villa is unclear in the sources.

It is a good place to think about how the town uses famous names. The Casino's guest list, the "X slept here" claims and Bram Stoker at Tihuța are the same pattern. Here at least the building and the name are real.
belvedere.s: istorielocala.ro (citing M. Vlădică, 2007); belvederedorna.ro; RRI (Oct 2025); en.wikipedia "Lucian Blaga"

p: The spa park behind the Casino is a 50 ha dendrological reserve and the town's main cluster of springs. It is famous for its tame red squirrels. Walk it for the music kiosk, a Japanese pavilion and an avenue of busts of Romanian writers and patriots (Eminescu, Costache Negri, Porumbescu and others), placed from 1964 onward. That date is worth noticing: the regime filled the Habsburg spa park with national heroes.
In mid-December the park and the Casino street host the Christmas events. The big winter-customs festival, with mask troupes and carollers, is held on 28–29 December.

The small station in the centre, "Băi" meaning "Baths", was built in 1910 on the left bank of the Dorna so that spa guests could step off the train almost at the Casino door. It is a listed monument and still in use, with an old-fashioned platform view over the river.

The line had reached the town's main station in 1902. The spa then pushed for this extension, and Băi was the end of the line until 1939, when the track was carried on toward Ilva Mică and Transylvania. That 1938–39 line, with 9 tunnels and 12 viaducts, was dynamited in 1944 and rebuilt by 1947. It is the best train ride from here.

Look at the east wall of this brick church on Str. Mihai Eminescu: three projectile tubes are set into the masonry. During the First World War, Russian artillery on the Mestecăniș front shelled the town. Three heavy shells hit this church and failed to explode. When it was repaired after the war, the parish set the casings into the wall at the points of impact as a reminder. It is Vatra Dornei's version of Athens' bullet holes.

The church was built in 1895–1905 on the site of a chapel of 1853, which was moved to the Catholic cemetery, and consecrated in 1905. It served the town's Catholic minority: German-speaking, Polish and Ukrainian railway and timber workers and officials. A 1917 photo shows its tower damaged. Its parish priest from 1905 to 1926, Iulius Veber, also served as the town's mayor in 1917–18, during the war.

The story comes from the local historian Paul Brașcanu, reported in 2018. Check in person which tubes are still visible; they may be easy to miss in the brick. The church is open for services and is well kept.
catholic-church.s: ercis.ro (2018, citing P. Brașcanu); Google reviews

p: The town hall (1897, in a Florentine palazzo style) and the obelisk in the park beside it are the civic centre of the Habsburg town. The obelisk is a war memorial of 1936, put up by a former mayor, Petru Forfotă: three stepped blocks, a three-part shaft, an eagle with open wings on top. On three faces it lists 89 Romanian dead of the First World War. On the fourth it lists 33 "co-inhabiting minority heroes", many of them Jewish names.

Read the monument for its edits. Before 1989 the eagle held a cross in its beak; under communism the cross was removed. Ceremonies were moved to the regime's dates: 9 May, 23 August and 25 October. After 2000 it was clad in marble and the cross restored. A column above the eagle lists the dead of 1941–45. The count of names has also drifted over the years, from 124 in an old photo album to 122 today.

The Ethnographic Museum on the Primăria's ground floor (Tue–Sun 10–16, about 10 lei) holds costume, masks and the raftsmen's tools. On Saturdays around midday there is often a șezătoare, a traditional craft-and-song gathering. Marble plaques listing every mayor "since 1650", with priest Veber as the 17th, are reported in town; the Primăria is the likely place (unconfirmed).
heroes-monument.s: ercis.ro (2018); LMI SV-II-m-B-05662; county tourism portal

p: The town's cultural centre since 1952, opposite the Primăria, named after Platon Pardău (1934–2002), a poet and prose writer born in Vatra Dornei. It is the room where the town's literary life happens now. A monthly cafenea literară (literary café) is run here by the local branch of the Arboroasa society. In mid-December it hosts the Christmas fair.

Arboroasa is a name with history. The original was a Romanian students' society in Habsburg Czernowitz in the 1870s. Today's group is a modern association that borrowed the name, not a continuation. The building is described as of architectural value but is not listed. Look inside for 1950s–80s socialist décor if a door is open.

This listed building at the start of Str. Mihai Eminescu sums up the town's owners in one façade. It was built around 1910 by the Church Fund of Bukovina as a rest home for Orthodox clergy. After 1956 it became the headquarters of the state mining enterprise that ran the basin's manganese and sulphur. In 2004 it went back to the Church.

The Church Fund matters here. It owned the baths, the springs, the forests and much of the land of Habsburg Bukovina, and it is the same body that bought the bankrupt Manz mining empire at Iacobeni in 1869. Under communism the mines took over its rest home. In 1939 the town's old wooden Orthodox church was moved next to this house, and it burned down in 1954 (see St Elias).
casa-vladimir.s: LMI SV-II-m-B-05661; Monitorul de Dorna; daibau.ro

p: The listed hotel at the corner of Eminescu and Gării is a building out of use. It opened as a hotel (sources give 1896 or 1927) and was nationalised in 1949. It ran as the state "Hotel Dorna" until 1995, then housed the court and the gendarmerie, and has had no maintenance since 1996. Don't confuse it with today's four-star Hotel Dorna on Str. Tudor Vladimirescu.

One source gives the same address to Vila Cembra (1895), a villa refitted in 1975 "with a touch of communist architecture" for the trade unions. Check on Street View or on site which building is which.
hotel-dorna-old.s: Monitorul de Dorna; LMI SV-II-m-B-05665; Europa Liberă. Map pin approximate

p: An Orthodox church in Moldavian style that started life as the Lutheran church of Dorna's Germans, built in 1905. The Germans left in 1940, when Bukovina's German communities were resettled to the Reich. The Romanian state compensated them and gave the church to the Orthodox parish in 1947, which enlarged it in 1984–93 into its present shape.
It stands two doors from the Great Synagogue. In one block you have the town's three lost minorities: Germans, Jews and, a few streets south at St Elias, Ruthenians.
nativity-church.s: Google reviews quoting the parish history; overview report

p: A large, decaying synagogue of about 1898–1902 on Str. Mihai Eminescu, visible from three sides and not in use. In 1930, 1,737 of the town's 7,759 people were Jewish. Jewish hoteliers had helped build the 19th-century spa, and Vizhnitz Hasidim kept a prayer house here.

The end came in stages. In 1918, after Bukovina joined Romania, there were riots: one Jew was killed and Jewish homes were burned. From the 1930s the town was a regional centre of antisemitic politics. In 1941 the region's Jews were concentrated in a ghetto here, and on 11 October 1941 they were deported to Transnistria from Gara Mare. People who tried to hide in this synagogue were dragged out. Bullet holes in its blue ceiling were reported visible until about 2000; whether restoration kept them is not known. A memorial plaque was placed here and at the station in October 2016.

After the war some survivors and refugees returned, and about 1,500 Jews lived in the town in 1947. Emigration followed, and only nine remained in 2003. Stand back on the street side for the whole façade. There is no regular access.
great-synagogue.s: Encyclopaedia Judaica (via Jewish Virtual Library); INSHR "Elie Wiesel"; Adevărul (Oct 2016); ro.wikipedia via D2. Map pin approximate

catholic-cemetery.t: Catholic cemetery: the Austrian soldier's grave
p: Among the graves is a crude stone cross that locals call "the Austrian soldier's grave". The letters run together, some are missing, and an S is carved backwards. It reads, in German, "Here rests our beloved son" Maxsa Iler, born 20 April 1890 in Tyrol, died at Dorna Watra on 22 March 1915, "for his fatherland". It was plainly cut by someone who did not write German, perhaps a local mason working from a note.

The war reached Dorna in its first winter, when Russian troops pushed into Bukovina. It came back in 1916–17, when the front ran along the Mestecăniș ridge above the town. The same cemetery holds the 1853 chapel that once stood where the Catholic church is, and the grave of Fr. Iulius Veber (died 1929), parish priest and wartime mayor.
The improved reading of the inscription is by the priest Iosif Răchiteanu. Ask locally for the grave's exact spot.

A small wooden church in a cemetery yard on the way up to the chairlift. It was built in 1908 as the Greek-Catholic church of the town's Ruthenians (Ukrainians), dedicated to the Transfiguration. It is the clearest trace of that community.

In 1948 the communist state banned the Greek-Catholic Church and handed its buildings to the Orthodox. A parish account repeated in reviews adds a darker detail. The town's old wooden Orthodox church, moved in 1939 next to Casa Vladimir, burned down on the night of 2 September 1954, in a fire apparently set up by the authorities. After that this Greek-Catholic church was given to the Orthodox. Treat the arson claim as unconfirmed. The church was reconsecrated on 1 November 2009.
st-elias.s: overview report; parish account via Google reviews (address Negrești 23)

p: On the slope along Str. Negrești, the cemetery of the community that helped build the spa. Its stones carry Hebrew, German and Romanian, the three languages of Habsburg Dorna.

It is usually locked. A visitor reports that the key is kept by the family at no. 34; ask politely. This is the companion to the Great Synagogue and the deportation plaque at Gara Mare: together they are the whole story.
jewish-cemetery.s: overview report; Google review; JewishGen cemetery project (photos 2012, 2016)

p: A 1980 chairlift that climbs about 3 km from 860 m to about 1,300 m in roughly 25 minutes of open chairs. It gives the only view over the whole Dorna basin: the town at the meeting of the Dorna and the Golden Bistrița, the Călimani volcanic massif to the south, the Suhard and Rarău ridges to the north.

Its name, "Black Hill", appears in the Manz family's list of iron-ore areas around 1800, and manganese deposits lie along the town's eastern edge. The ring of mining is visible from the top if you know where to look. Iacobeni and Arșița are north, and the Călimani sulphur scar is south, on a clear day.

Practical: 10:00–16:30 daily, last ride up around 16:00. About 50 lei return, 30 lei one way. It needs a minimum number of riders and stops in strong wind or fog, so call 0744 587 537. It is cold in late autumn. Many people ride up and walk down.
chairlift.s: operator page; judetulsuceava.ro; Google reviews (2025–26); Analele Bucovinei (Manz study)

p: The main station of 1902, where the railway first reached Dorna, is also the town's place of departure in the worst sense. On 11 October 1941, about 2,650 Jews from the town and nearby villages were loaded into cattle wagons in two trains, on the same day, and sent to Transnistria. A plaque put up on 6 October 2016 by the Federation of Jewish Communities and the Elie Wiesel Institute records it. Its text says that 91,845 Jews were deported from Bukovina in autumn 1941 on the orders of Ion Antonescu.

A second plaque, from January 2014, honours Emanuel A. Ziffer (1833–1913), a Jewish engineer and honorary citizen of Czernowitz, then Bukovina's capital. He built some 580 km of local railways in Bukovina, including this line. Ziffer was a friend of Mayor Deac, and local historians call him "the father of the Bukovina railways". So the same station carries both the town's modernisation and its deportation, each marked by a Jew.

The figures differ by source: one encyclopedia gives 2,029 deported from the town itself, with 21 left behind. An Interior Ministry file records that in June 1942, 12 families deported on 11 October were allowed to return. The station today has no ticket office or waiting room. Find the plaques; their exact spot was not confirmed.
gara-mare.s: INSHR "Elie Wiesel"; Adevărul (Oct 2016); Realitatea Evreiască 422–423 (Feb 2014); Encyclopaedia Judaica; EHRI portal (file 104/41)

p: A terraced war cemetery on the hillside near Gara Mare: rows of plain concrete crosses, nearly all reading Erou Necunoscut (Unknown Hero), under a tall oak cross of 1937. You reach it through the old Evangelical cemetery of the town's Germans.

It holds both sides of the First World War. A 1931 count recorded 246 dead: 115 Romanians, 130 Austro-Hungarian soldiers and one German. Only six graves have names. The cemetery is said to have been laid out in 1917, while the front still ran on the hills above. The 1937 cross was dedicated by the Străjeri, the royal youth movement of King Carol II.
Walk the terraces and then the German graves at the entrance: a compact lesson in how a Habsburg border town was buried. The site is open at all times.
heroes-cemetery.s: Oficiul Național pentru Cultul Eroilor (via D1); Google review

calimani-sulphur.t: Călimani sulphur quarry and the ghost colony
p: High above Gura Haitii, at about 1,500–2,000 m, the communist state cut away the side of a volcano. The quarry at Negoiul Românesc was Romania's only open-pit mine for native sulphur. Today it is a stepped, red-and-yellow crater with four waste dumps, a smell of sulphur, and lumps of bright yellow native sulphur still lying among the stones near Pietricelul peak. Visitors describe it as another planet.

Serious work began in 1969 under the geologist Emil Butnaru. The south-east slope was stripped from 1970 to 1992, and the mine closed in 1997. A small town was built beside it, with blocks, canteens, shops, a cinema and even a kindergarten. Workers who were not local lived there or in blocks down at Neagra Șarului. Figures for the workforce range from 2,000 to 8,000. Ceaușescu landed by helicopter in winter 1981, and youth brigades were sent up in 1981 and 1983. Natural sulphur caves called Luana's Grottoes and the "Chocolate Palace" were destroyed by the digging. Most specialists say the mine lost money throughout.

After closure the dumps were covered and the colony mostly demolished in a clean-up. What survives is the derelict "protocol villa" built for Ceaușescu in a forest clearing below Rețițiș peak: two floors, a big living room with a fireplace, parquet and tiles, central heating and a helipad. Locals say he used it twice. Accounts of who saved it differ: a local buyer, or engineers who thought it too solid to knock down. The Neagra river below is still polluted.

Practical: from Gura Haitii, about 12–15 km of broken concrete road (DJ174F) at 30–40 km/h to a car park below the quarry. The blue-cross trail takes about an hour to the top. From November snow can close it; go only in dry weather, ideally with a high-clearance car or a guide.
calimani-sulphur.s: carpati.org; calimani.ro (trail 2 PDF); svnews.ro; Adevărul; Monitorul de Suceava (2008, 2011); dornabike.ro; Scînteia Tineretului (Jul 1983); Google reviews

p: South of Gura Negrei, between Șarul peak and the Sărișorul brook, is a walled hollow where carbon dioxide rises through the water in large bubbles: the La Cruce ("At the Cross") spring. Its water contains arsenic. For almost a century it was bottled and sold as a healing water, under the name "Carmen Sylva", the pen name of Romania's poet-queen Elisabeth.

The arsenic is the story. The village takes its name from șar, a reddish ground rich in arsenic that was once dug and sent to Austria. In 1788 Hacquet found a half-collapsed arsenic-sulphide pit here, guarded by an imperial picket. The guards were reportedly there to stop locals using the arsenic to poison wells. The water was analysed repeatedly from 1833. One 1890s analysis gives 0.00177 g of arsenic oxide per litre. Romania's Sanitary Council approved it as a medicinal and table water in 1890, and it was exported to France from 1894. In 1892 the bacteriologist Victor Babeș found no pathogenic germs and called it among the cleanest waters in Europe. After a medical commission found high arsenic and metaboric acid in 1982, a letter of 14 July 1986 asked for the bottling unit to be closed for good.

Locals still use the springs, and the bottling plant is said to be gone (unverified). For context first, the Călimani National Park visitor centre in Șaru Dornei (weekdays 10–14) explains the volcanic geology and the mineral waters, with tastings. The map pin is approximate: ask at the visitor centre.
saru-springs.s: Monitorul de Dorna (P. Brașcanu, 13 Oct 2015); dragusanul.ro (1902 geographical dictionary); Google Places. Map pin approximate

p: On the hillside above Iacobeni is a quarry about 2.4 km² across, opened into old manganese workings, with at least three gallery mouths showing in its walls. The mineral collectors' database Mindat calls it a manganese "madness". Dolomite was still being quarried here in 2020, so look from outside, not inside.

Arșița was an iron mine of the Manz family from the 1790s. After their bankruptcy in 1859 it was converted to manganese, and in the socialist period the area was said to produce about 98% of Romania's manganese. Iacobeni also had the country's only manganese-salts plant, with about 500 workers, used for fertiliser and steel. It closed around 1994, and the mines closed in 1997. The adits have names: Theresia and Sahara.
arsita.s: mindat.org; Ziarul de Iași; svnews.ro; georeview.usv.ro

p: In Iacobeni stands the abandoned manor, built in 1823, of the family that founded modern mining in Bukovina, with its service pavilion in the same state. The local news site svnews revisited it in June 2026: three years after its first report, nothing had been done, and the building is in advanced decay.

In 1796 Anton Manz von Mariensee, an industrialist from Styria, bought the Iacobeni ironworks for 300,000 florins. He brought German miners from the Zips region of today's Slovakia, built about 280 miners' houses (about 200 said to survive), a company store and a mine office. He founded colonies across the mountains, among them Mariensee (Cârlibaba). His nephew Vincenz, trained at the Schemnitz mining academy, enlarged the "Margareta" and "Iosif" furnaces and built the village's Gothic church in 1828 to plans from Vienna. Overextended, the business went bankrupt in 1859. The Church Fund bought it in 1869 and the furnaces were closed.

The 1828 church is pinned. The sources call it Lutheran but dedicate it to St John of Nepomuk, a Catholic saint, so check which it is on site. The manor has no published address; ask in the village. Iacobeni also lay on the WWI military railway that Russian prisoners built over the Prislop pass in 1915–16, the highest railway ever built in the Carpathians, dismantled in 1930–31.
manz-manor.s: svnews.ro (2023; 7 Jun 2026); Analele Bucovinei (O. Bâtă on the Manz family); dragusanul.ro; ro.wikipedia. Map pin approximate

ciocanesti.t: Ciocănești: the painted village and egg museum
p: A village on the Golden Bistrița where more than 600 houses are painted outside with the patterns of local costume and painted eggs. Since 2003–04 the commune has called itself a "museum commune", and painting the façades is required. The National Painted Egg Museum in the cultural centre holds over 3,000 eggs, the oldest more than a century old. Across the road the ethnographic museum has rooms on smithing, mining, shepherding and rafting.

The rafting room links back to the industrial story. Timber left the Dorna basin by raft down the Bistrița, with dams (haituri) releasing floods to carry the logs. The stone for the Mestecăniș tunnel was rafted from here. Rafts are still floated at the August trout festival.
Practical: the egg museum is open Mon–Fri 10–16, Sat 11–15, Sun 13–16. Egg-painting demonstrations can be arranged.
ciocanesti.s: RRI; suceava.online; Adevărul; taradornelor.ro; Google Places

p: The railway into Vatra Dornei passes under the Mestecăniș ridge through a crest tunnel of about 1,622 m (1,646.6 m with portals), opened in October 1902 by the Bukovina local railway company. You experience it by train: the line from Câmpulung Moldovenesc runs through it.

It was bombed at both ends in the Second World War and reopened in 1946. A second bore was driven in 1976–79, and its engineer, Corneliu Hădăreanu, later told the railway magazine Club Feroviar a fine socialist story: the official breakthrough blast, staged for the press and state television, happened three days before the rock was actually holed through. The date the second bore opened is given as 1979 or 1985.
mestecanis-tunnel.s: Crai Nou; ro.wikipedia; clubferoviar.ro; trenuriromania blog

p: Beside the hillside Catholic church of Cârlibaba Nouă is a mass grave of Polish Legion soldiers: Captain Stanisław Strzelecki and eleven legionaries, killed in January 1915 fighting the Russians for the Carpathian passes. Strzelecki was shot in the head on 19 January. The monument dates from 1932 and was renewed in 2007 with a bilingual plaque.

The church itself, St Louis (1890–1900), was built for the Zipser German miners of the Mariensee colony. The Manz company founded the colony in 1797 to work silver-bearing galena on Fluturica mountain. The bricks were made by a group of Roma who then moved on. A German war cemetery (Heldenfriedhof Kirlibaba) is also recorded nearby. The Dadu manganese mine, closed in 1997, is just up the valley.
carlibaba-polish.s: svnews.ro; en.wikipedia; historia.ro; denkmalprojekt.org; Analele Bucovinei

castel-dracula.t: Tihuța Pass: Castel Dracula and the war railway
p: At 1,201 m on the road to Bistrița stands a mock-medieval hotel, built in 1976–83 as Hotel Tihuța to cash in on Bram Stoker's "Borgo Pass". Its fake graveyard and "Dracula's tomb" cellar were part of the act, and a bust of Stoker has stood outside since 2006. It has been closed since November 2019. A Bistrița builder bought it in 2020 for €1.6 million, and no reopening has been announced.

The record is plainer than the legend. Stoker never went to Romania. His notes, now at the Rosenbach in Philadelphia, show he took Bistritz and Borgo Prund from his reading. The real history of the pass is industrial. In 1916 more than 5,500 prisoners of war built a 33 km petrol-electric military railway over it from Dornișoara to Tiha Bârgăului. Locomotives were dismantled to get them across. After an accident and little traffic it closed on 23 June 1939, and the rails were removed in the Second World War. Parts of the route can still be traced near the old Tihuța halt.
Combine it with Tinovul Mare at Poiana Stampei on the way: a 681 ha peat bog, 8,000–9,000 years old, with a free boardwalk and carnivorous sundews.
castel-dracula.s: romaniaatlas.com; Infobistrita; Monitorul de Dorna; ro.wikipedia; Club Feroviar album; judetulsuceava.ro

dorna-candrenilor.t: Dorna Candrenilor: the spa that came back
p: A village spa about 7 km west that died in the 1930s and reopened in the 2020s. Its first baths, founded by Cosma Donisă, opened around 1898–99 with copper tubs, and between the wars the spa was known across Europe. Sources disagree on whether it was destroyed in 1914 or burned in 1937. The last mayor to keep it going, Ilie Ursu, did so in 1937. A 26 ha park survived.

By July 2025 a new spa centre was running, with four pools, saunas and a salt room, open daily 10:00–21:30. The mayor has promised to revive the traditional borcut (mineral-water) baths and mud cures. For the chemist, the F6 borehole is the sight: 110 m deep, reopened after about 32 years in conservation, it erupts in bursts as carbon dioxide drives the mineral water up. A reporter called the eruption "extremely spectacular". Ask where it is.
dorna-candrenilor.s: moldovainvest.eu (MREF, Jul 2025); Monitorul de Suceava; Monitorul de Dorna; SuceavaLIVE; Google Places

p: The factory that fills Romania's best-known mineral water. Coca-Cola HBC has owned it since 2002, with about 250 staff. It bottles Dorna, Dorna Izvorul Alb and Dorna Poiana Negri. Dorna water itself is piped from Poiana Vinului at Coșna. Local bottling goes back to 1923. Under the Habsburgs, villagers did forced labour carrying barrels of this water. Exterior only: there are no tours.
poiana-negrii.s: Economedia; HotNews; comunacosna.ro; Monitorul de Dorna

p: A small museum of the Dorna basin's animals and plants, founded in 1956 and reopened in September 2026 after an energy refit. It has brown bears, capercaillie, a bearded vulture, edelweiss and other protected flora, and a winter diorama of a stag attacked by wolves that the museum calls unique in Romania.

Good for the biologist's eye: the fauna of the Călimani and Suhard ranges in one room, plus the hunting-trophy tradition of a Habsburg forest estate. Tue–Fri 10–17, Sat–Sun 10–14, about 5 lei. Labels are in Romanian.
natural-sciences.s: Suceava News Online (Sep 2026); suceava.online; Google reviews

p: The large Orthodox cathedral at the entrance to the spa park, built 1991–2002, with seven towers for the seven sacraments. It is the post-1989 answer to the Habsburg spa: the Church took back the Casino and the springs' old owner, the Church Fund, and built itself a cathedral next to them.
Services are relayed by loudspeaker into the street. Frescoes 1999–2002. A short stop.

A small centre in Șaru Dornei on the Călimani volcano: a big model of the 10 km caldera, panels on the rock layers and vegetation belts, and a section on why the basin's mineral waters form here, with tastings of local waters. It is the best briefing before the sulphur quarry or the arsenic springs.

Open weekdays 10:00–14:00 (a 2024 visitor found it less cared for than before, and the outdoor area damaged). Staff sell trail maps and give advice on the Călimani routes; the park runs guided trips in season.
calimani-centre.s: Google Places and reviews (2024); overview report

p: A 681 ha raised peat bog at Poiana Stampei, 8,000–9,000 years old, crossed by a wooden boardwalk of about 900 m. You walk through bog pine and birch over sphagnum, past carnivorous sundews. It was declared a natural monument in 1955 after studies by the botanist Emil Pop.
Free and open at all times; about 20 km toward Bistrița, then about 4 km of forest road from the village. The boards are slippery with frost. Information panels are in Romanian only.

The only manganese mine in Romania you can enter: a gallery near Ciocănești where you put on rubber boots, a helmet and a miner's lamp and walk into rock at 3 °C. The guide is usually a former miner, and the greeting is the miners' noroc bun! (good luck). Inside you see the dynamite store and a working face left as it was when the mine closed.

The mine had 15 galleries and sent 200–300 tonnes of ore a day to the Galați steelworks. It was put into conservation in 2000 and reopened for visitors in August 2014. The plan was 800 m of gallery, later 1.5 km; in practice visits often go about 50 m in.
Practical: groups only, by appointment through the Țara Dornelor tourism office. A 7 km marked loop trail starts opposite the Ciocănești church. Combine it with the egg museum.
oita-mine.s: Lumea Satului; Monitorul de Suceava (Aug 2014); taradornelor.ro; kids-exploring.com (Nov 2024). Map pin unknown

japanese-pavilion.t: Pavilionul Japonez, the busts and the squirrels
p: Every Romanian guide sends you here first. Inside the central spa park (the town's 50 ha dendrological reserve) stand the Pavilionul Japonez, a 1925 bandstand named for its Japanese-style roof, by the lake, and an alley of busts of Romanian cultural figures: Eminescu, Caragiale, Sadoveanu, Enescu, Porumbescu, Kogălniceanu, Costache Negri and Alecu Russo. The pavilion is a listed monument and was restored a few years ago.

The park is known to Romanians as the "Squirrel Park". The red squirrels are tame and still active in autumn; nuts are sold in bags at the entrance, and locals say you call them by tapping two walnuts together. Taste the free mineral water at the park fountains on the way.
The park's founding date is disputed: one source says 1862, others the end of the 19th century. It was declared a reserve in 1970. Summer concerts in the pavilion don't run in November.
japanese-pavilion.s: pierdutiinvacanta.ro; vatra-dornei.info; Știrile ProTV; CIMEC postcards; 2Turiști și Jumătate (2025)

p: Runc hill (1,149 m) rises straight above the north side of town and is the first belvedere on the classic Suhard ridge trail. From the top you see the whole Dorna basin, the meeting of the rivers and, on the ridge behind, Oușoru (1,639 m) and Fărăoane.

The trail starts beside the church at the foot of Runc (Strada Runc area): about 15–20 minutes' walk from the centre, then 20–25 minutes up on red and blue band markings. A longer loop of about 2 hours (≈300 m of climb) starts at the Dorna footbridge by the park and comes back along the Drumul Tătarilor. The hill has a park from Austro-Hungarian times, ski runs and a small camping area.

If you'd rather not climb, the flat Drumul Tătarilor ("Tatars' Road") gravel track runs along the foot of Runc beside the Dorna towards the hamlet of Popeni. The tourist information centre (Str. Gării 2, +40 230 372 767) has current trail conditions and runs guided Suhard hikes.

Vatra Dornei is first of all a ski town, and these are its in-town slopes. Veverița opened in 2011: 850 m long, with night lighting and snowmaking. The Parc slope is the beginners' run, reached straight from the centre. With the long Dealul Negru run under the chairlift there are four slopes in all.

In November they are closed. Last season Veverița opened on 2 January 2026. A single ski pass covers Veverița and Parc; previous seasons cost about 150–170 lei a day for adults. The February Snow Festival is held on Veverița. Pin position is approximate.
veverita.s: Știrile ProTV; Monitorul de Suceava; suceava.online

p: The stock answer to "where do we eat traditional food?": Casa Bucovineană, at Str. Vasile Deac 2 on the corner with Calea Transilvaniei. It bakes its own bread and plays traditional music daily. Order ciorbă de burtă (tripe soup), tochitură or sarmale.

It gets crowded and reviews are good rather than great (about 4.0 on Google). Restaurant Dorna at the four-star Hotel Dorna (Str. Tudor Vladimirescu 5A) is the other usual recommendation, with ciorbă rădăuțeană and wild-boar stew. For local cheese (telemea, caș, brânză de burduf), the town market is on Str. Mihail Kogălniceanu (hours unverified).

A convent at Str. Chiliei 11B, on the right bank of the Bistrița towards Dorna Arini. The street name (chilia, a monk's cell) recalls the hermitage that stood here. It was built in 1997–2003 and consecrated on 7 December 2003, with paintings by Viorel Costan; the first nuns came from Dragomirna. An old people's home run by a local foundation works inside.

The official Țara Dornelor site lists it first under spirituality, but it is a secondary sight: one travel writer says it won't impress anyone who has seen Voroneț. Take it on the way to Dorna Arini. Pin position is approximate.

The Protection of the Mother of God monastery stands at the foot of Bârnărel hill in Gheorghițeni village, about 5 km towards Piatra Neamț on the left bank of the Bistrița. Everything is built of wood, including a very tall bell tower (one source says 60 m; unverified).

It is new: consecrated on 20 October 2004 by the Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew together with Romania's Patriarch Teoctist. Its feast day is 1 October and it has guest rooms. It is the easy first stop on the road to the Zugreni gorges.

The Bistrița cuts through the mountains here between Sunători and Chiril in a gorge about 2.5 km long (one source says 4 km), with rock walls 200–300 m high and named crags such as Colțul Acrii, Piatra lui Osman and Stânca Coifului. It is a nature reserve and Natura 2000 site, home to edelweiss and the rare huchen (lostriță), a protected Danube salmon.

You see it from the road (about 25 minutes by car), which also makes it the scenic approach to Chiril and Rarău. In summer it is the town's rafting stretch (Dorna Adventure, Str. Chilia 4); in November treat rafting as unavailable unless the operator confirms.

pietrele-doamnei.t: Rarău: Pietrele Doamnei and Rarău monastery
p: Pietrele Doamnei are the emblem of the Rarău massif: limestone towers up to 70 m tall standing above 1,600 m. The pin is the car park at Hotel Alpin Rarău; from there a blue-cross circuit of 1.5–2 hours goes round the rocks, with chains on the top section. In November expect ice and snow, and view the towers from the base if conditions are poor.

Rarău monastery, at nearly 1,400 m, goes back by tradition to a 15th-century hermitage of the monk Sisoe. Petru Rareș built a church after his wife and children took refuge with the monks in 1538; a new church was consecrated in 2000.

Getting there: about 55 km, 1 h 15–1 h 30 by car via Pojorâta (towards Câmpulung, then about 16 km of mountain road). The Chiril–Rarău road (Transrarău) is closed every winter once snow falls. Check with the information centre before going. Pair it with Câmpulung's museums.

campulung-museums.t: Câmpulung Moldovenesc: Wood Art and spoon museums
p: The best bad-weather day trip, 45 km away (about 50 minutes, also on the railway). The Muzeul Arta Lemnului (Calea Transilvaniei 10) shows more than 15,000 wooden objects in 20 rooms, from tools to furniture, with an open-air section of traditional wooden houses. It was refurbished in 2017–21. Winter hours from 1 November: Tue–Sun 9:00–17:00, last entry 16:30; adults 20 lei, guided tour 50 lei; phone 0230 311 378.

The Ion Țugui spoon collection (Str. Gheorghe Popovici 1) fills a late history teacher's house with more than 6,000 wooden spoons from Romania and 30+ countries, plus 500 woven towels. His granddaughter gives the tours. Entry is a donation; hours conflict between sources, so phone 0230 311 315 first. The pin is approximate.

voronet.t: Voroneț: the "Sistine Chapel of the East"
p: The painted monasteries are the top attraction of all Bukovina, and the single biggest gap the classics check found. Voroneț (1488, painted outside in 1547) is the famous one: the west wall is covered by a huge Last Judgement, and the intense blue background is known as "Voroneț blue". The churches of Moldavia were inscribed by UNESCO in 1993.

It is about 75 km from Vatra Dornei (around 1 h 30 by car), near Gura Humorului, which is on the railway. Off-season hours are 9:00–17:00; entry 10 lei, 10 lei more to photograph outside, no photos inside. Dress modestly; a free guide is available on request outside service times.
In November, with sunset around 16:30, plan two or three monasteries a day, not five: Voroneț with Humor, or Moldovița with Sucevița.

Humor's church (1530) is one of the UNESCO painted churches, its frescoes dominated by red-ochre tones rather than Voroneț's blue. It is about 6 km north of Gura Humorului, so it pairs naturally with Voroneț on a short November day. Entry about 10 lei. Pin position is approximate.

The closest painted monastery to Vatra Dornei, about 60 km away (sources say 59–63 km), over the mountains via Sadova. Prince Petru Rareș built it in 1532 inside fortified walls. Its best-known scene is the Siege of Constantinople, painted as a contemporary event at a time when the Ottomans pressed on Moldavia.
Go with Sucevița, 30 minutes further over the Ciumârna pass, for the natural two-monastery November day. Entry about 10 lei.

Sucevița (1580s) is the latest and most complete of the painted monasteries, behind high fortress walls with corner towers. Its north wall carries the Ladder of Virtues: angels help the righteous up thirty rungs to heaven while devils drag sinners off into the dark. Its church was added to the UNESCO site in 2010.
It sits over the Ciumârna pass from Moldovița. From here Putna, Stephen the Great's burial place, is another 30 minutes north if daylight allows.

Stephen the Great founded Putna in 1466–69 and is buried in its church, which makes it one of Romania's most important pilgrimage sites. It is not painted outside like the others. It has a museum of medieval embroidery and manuscripts. It is the far end of the loop, about 30 minutes north of Sucevița; entry by donation.

Weathered pillars of volcanic agglomerate on the Călimani plateau, which locals have read as the twelve apostles and other figures (one is called the Marshal). It is one of the area's top-ranked nature sights.

Drive about 25–28 km via Dorna Arini and Șaru Dornei to Gura Haitii (about 40 minutes), take the signed forest road and walk about 1 km to a carved wooden gate, then follow the blue-dot trail. Out and back takes 4–6 hours; a loop via Pietrele Roșii is about 13.6 km with 730 m of climb. In November go only on a clear, snow-free day and start by 9:00 to be down before dark. Pin position is approximate.

Oușoru is the peak you keep seeing from town, at the end of the Suhard ridge. From Vatra Dornei the trail runs over Vârful Runc to the foot of Oușoru in about 3 hours (blue band); the whole return hike is 4–5 hours. A shorter route (blue cross) starts at the church at the entrance to Dorna Candrenilor, about 3 hours one way.
The information centre (Str. Gării 2) runs guided hikes, 5–6 hours, about 300 lei per group. In November treat it as conditional. Pin position is approximate.

routes.name: Spa core: the Casino, the springs and the cure
routes.when: The Casino is shut Mon–Tue; the rest is open any day.
routes.summary: The Habsburg spa in 800 m: the Casino, Sentinela, the Unirea spring and bath house, the socialist cure hotels, Blaga's villa and the spa station.

routes.name: Eminescu Street: four faiths and the civic town
routes.when: Ethnographic Museum Tue–Sun; synagogue exterior only.
routes.summary: West along the old main street: the shelled Catholic church, the town hall and its edited war memorial, the culture house, the clergy home that became the mining HQ, and the ex-Lutheran church beside the Great Synagogue.

routes.name: Negrești Street: cemeteries up to the chairlift
routes.when: Chairlift 10:00–16:30, weather permitting; Jewish cemetery key at no. 34.
routes.summary: Uphill past the Austrian soldier's grave, the Ruthenian wooden church and the Jewish cemetery, then the chairlift for the whole basin.

routes.name: North: Gara Mare and the heroes' cemetery
routes.summary: The 1902 station with the 1941 deportation and Ziffer plaques, then the terraced WWI cemetery behind the Germans' graves.

routes.name: Day trip: Iacobeni, the Manz mining empire
routes.when: Outside views only; the Arșița quarry may be partly active.
routes.summary: North up the Golden Bistrița: the 1823 Manz manor and 1828 church, the Arșița manganese quarry, and the Mestecăniș tunnel on the train line. Half a day.

routes.name: Day trip: Ciocănești and Cârlibaba
routes.when: Egg museum Mon–Fri 10–16, Sat 11–15, Sun 13–16; Oița mine by appointment.
routes.summary: The painted village and egg museum (with the Oița mine if booked), then on to the Polish Legion grave and the Zipser miners' church at Cârlibaba.

routes.name: Day trip: Călimani, sulphur and arsenic
routes.when: Visitor centre weekdays 10–14; the quarry road can close with snow from November.
routes.summary: The volcano's chemistry in a day: the park visitor centre, the arsenic springs of Șaru Dornei, then 12–15 km of broken concrete road to the sulphur quarry and Ceaușescu's villa.

routes.name: Day trip: west to the Tihuța Pass
routes.when: Castel Dracula closed since 2019; Tinovul Mare free.
routes.summary: Along DN17: the reborn spa of Dorna Candrenilor, the Dorna bottling plant, the Tinovul Mare bog, and the fake Dracula castle on the real WWI railway pass.

routes.name: Town classics: the park and Runc hill
routes.when: Free; Runc is muddy or icy after rain or snow.
routes.summary: The spa park's Japanese pavilion, busts and squirrels, lunch at Casa Bucovineană, then up Runc hill for the view over the whole basin.

routes.name: Day trip: the painted monasteries
routes.when: 9:00–17:00 off-season; in November pick two or three.
routes.summary: Bukovina's UNESCO churches: Voroneț and Humor, or Moldovița and Sucevița, with Putna at the far end. About 220–260 km for the whole loop.

routes.name: Day trip: Câmpulung and Rarău
routes.when: Arta Lemnului closed Mondays; Rarău via Pojorâta only in winter.
routes.summary: The Wood Art and spoon museums in Câmpulung Moldovenesc, then up the Pojorâta road to the Pietrele Doamnei rocks and Rarău monastery.

routes.name: Day trip: east down the Bistrița
routes.summary: St Demetrius at the edge of town, the all-wood Dorna Arini monastery, then the 300 m walls of the Zugreni gorges. A half day.

tours.name: The water chain: from spa to arsenic
tours.intro: Carbon dioxide from the Călimani volcano turns ordinary groundwater into mineral water. Follow it from the polite spa to the closed arsenic springs.
tours.how: Town stops on foot; Dorna Candrenilor, Poiana Negrii and Șaru Dornei by car.
story: The town exists because of gas: CO₂ dissolving in river-terrace groundwater, picking up iron and minerals. The Habsburgs built a spa on it, the socialists a mass cure, Coca-Cola a bottling plant, and at Șaru Dornei a celebrated table water turned out to carry arsenic.

stops.note: The emblem spring; its three names track the century.
Where patients once drew their bath water.
The socialist cure: mofettes, a dry bath in CO₂.
The F6 borehole erupts with CO₂-driven water.
Today's industrial end: "Dorna" in plastic.
"Carmen Sylva" water, shut in 1986 for arsenic.
The volcano's plumbing laid open.

tours.name: Ore: the Manz empire to the sulphur mine
tours.intro: Two centuries of extraction in one basin: Habsburg iron, socialist manganese and sulphur, all closed by 1997.
tours.how: Mostly by car; Casa Vladimir and the chairlift are in town.
story: A Styrian family built an iron empire here in 1796 and went bankrupt in 1859. The Church Fund bought it; the socialist state turned the basin into Romania's manganese supply and cut a sulphur mine into a volcano.

stops.note: The founders' 1823 manor, decaying.
The great quarry, iron then manganese.
Cârlibaba was the Manz silver-lead colony; the church was built for its miners.
The town office of the state mining enterprise after 1956.
"Black Hill" was on the Manz list of iron-ore areas; view the whole ring from the top.
The last and biggest: open-pit sulphur, 1970–1997.

tours.name: The front of 1914–17
tours.intro: Russian guns on the ridge, prisoners building railways, and the dead of both sides.
tours.how: Four stops in town on foot; Cârlibaba and Tihuța by car.
story: Dorna sat on the Habsburg front twice: in the first winter and again in 1916–17, when the line ran along the Mestecăniș ridge above the town.

stops.note: Three Russian duds hit it; their casings are set in the wall.
A misspelled cross for a 24-year-old Tyrolean, 1915.
246 dead of both sides; nearly all "unknown".
The 1936 obelisk and its later edits.
Polish legionaries killed in January 1915.
The pass carried a 1916 military railway built by prisoners.

tours.name: The Jewish town and 1941
tours.intro: Jewish hoteliers helped build the spa; on 11 October 1941 the community was deported from the station.
tours.how: All on foot, about 3 km in total.
story: In 1930 more than a fifth of the town was Jewish. A Jewish engineer built its railway. The same station became the place of deportation to Transnistria.

stops.note: The decaying synagogue; people hiding here were dragged out in 1941.
Hebrew, German and Romanian stones; ask for the key.
33 minority war dead, many of them Jewish, on the fourth face.
The 2016 deportation plaque and the 2014 plaque to Ziffer, the railway builder.

tours.name: Myth and record: what the spa tells you
tours.intro: A spa sells stories. Three stops where the story and the record part ways.
tours.how: Belvedere and the Casino on foot; Tihuța by car.
story: The Blaga residence is impossible as dated, the Casino guest list unsourced, and Stoker never came near the Borgo Pass.

stops.note: "Blaga lived here 1952–64" — he died in 1961.
The famous visitors list has no traceable source.
A 1970s hotel built on a novel; the real pass history is a war railway.
